evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

In July 2013, the plaintiff allegedly was injured when she tripped and fell on a gap in a walkway adjacent to a strip mall owned by the defendant Garden Homes Management Corp. (hereinafter the defendant).

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant Garden Homes Management Corp. appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Orange County (Robert A. Onofry, J.), dated November 4, 2020. The order denied that defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.
Here, the defendant failed to demonstrate, prima facie, that the alleged condition was not inherently dangerous, that the alleged condition was trivial
or that it lacked actual or constructive notice of the alleged condition
The defendant therefore failed to shift the burden to the plaintiff to raise a triable issue of fact.

Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it without regard to the sufficiency of the opposition papers

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with costs, and that branch of the motion of the defendant Whispering Hills Home Owners Association, Inc., which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it is denied.

As is relevant to this appeal, in December 2018, the plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries she alleged that she sustained in March 2018 when she slipped and fell on ice on an exterior staircase within a condominium complex owned and managed by the defendant Whispering Hills Home Owners Association, Inc. (hereinafter the defendant).

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Orange County (Sandra B. Sciortino, J.), dated December 2, 2020. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted that branch of the motion of the defendant Whispering Hills Home Owners Association, Inc., which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

In support of its motion, the defendant submitted, inter alia, the deposition testimony of the plaintiff, who testified, among other things, that it was not snowing at the time that she fell on the icy stairs, which failed to eliminate triable issues of fact as to whether a storm was in progress at the time of the accident
whether the plaintiff slipped and fell on a preexisting condition, and whether the defendant had constructive notice of this condition

Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied that branch of the defendant's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it without regard to the sufficiency of the opposition papers

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the June 25, 2018 denial of summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: A USPS mail carrier slipped while descending interior stairs in a residential building allegedly owned and/or managed by defendants on December 2, 2014. She identified a wet, slippery substance as the cause but could not identify its precise composition.

legal_issues.finding: Plaintiff and superintendent depositions raised a factual issue whether defendants created the condition; the opinion does not describe a specific creation act.
Defendants supplied no specific pre-accident cleaning/inspection evidence and failed their initial burden regardless of plaintiff’s opposition.
Identifying a wet substance was sufficient to defeat defendants’ inability-to-identify-cause argument even though plaintiff did not know its exact composition.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition identified the wet substance and, with superintendent testimony, raised creation issues.
Superintendent’s deposition, submitted by defendants, contributed to the triable creation issue; no specific account is quoted.

quality.notes: The narrative expressly alleges ownership/management of the actual residential building, with superintendent and maintenance evidence, supporting private control while preserving allegation status. Roles describe collective owner/manager alternatives, not every defendant holding both. Plaintiff’s public-sector employment does not make the premises public. Unknown liquid composition is distinct from failure to identify the fall cause. Creation remains triable; no act, notice duration or inspection record is invented. The generic notice defense is not treated as a separately resolved actual-notice issue.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

On December 2, 2014, the plaintiff, then a mail carrier employed by the United States Postal Service, slipped and fell while descending an interior set of stairs in a residential building that allegedly was owned and/or managed by the defendants.
The plaintiff alleged that she slipped and fell due to a "wet and slippery substance" on the stairs.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Peter P. Sweeney, J.), dated June 25, 2018. The order denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

The plaintiff's deposition testimony identified the cause of her fall as a wet substance on the stairs. The plaintiff's mere inability to identify the precise nature of the wet substance upon which she allegedly slipped and fell cannot be equated with a failure to identify the cause of her fall

Moreover, the evidence submitted in support of the defendants' motion, especially the deposition transcripts of the plaintiff and the superintendent of the subject building, revealed triable issues of fact as to whether the defendants created the alleged condition

Furthermore, we agree with the Supreme Court's conclusion that the defendants failed to present evidence regarding any specific cleaning or inspection of the area in question relative to the time when the plaintiff's accident occurred
Since the defendants failed to meet their prima facie burden, we need not address the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers
Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination to deny the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.

The plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries allegedly sustained by her when she fell while descending an interior stairway within premises owned by the defendant and improved with a multiple dwelling.

In her complaint, the plaintiff asserted that she was at the premises visiting a friend in the basement of the building, when she fell down the interior stairway. The plaintiff contended that she slipped and fell because of poor lighting and the lack of a handrail.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Richmond County (McMahon, J.), entered April 4, 2013, which granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

The defendant's submissions in support of its motion included, among other things, a transcript of the deposition testimony of the plaintiff, in which the plaintiff testified that, as she was descending the stairs, she took one step with her right foot and "slipped," and that she "went to grab on, to try to hold [herself but] there was nothing to grab onto so [she] went all the way down." It is undisputed that the stairs in question were not furnished with a handrail.

The defendant failed to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, as its submissions failed to eliminate all triable issues of fact as to whether a handrail was statutorily required at the location where the plaintiff fell ( see Multiple Dwelling Law § 52; Administrative Code of City of NY § 27-375; Building Code of NY State § 1009.10, as incorporated by 19 NYCRR 1221.1 [a], [b];

Moreover, the plaintiff's deposition testimony, which was submitted by the defendant in support of [*2] its motion, revealed the existence of a triable issue of fact as to whether the lack of a handrail was a proximate cause of the plaintiff's injuries
Since the defendant failed to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, we need not consider the sufficiency of the opposing papers
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Following the completion of discovery, the defendant moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, arguing that it did not create the allegedly dangerous condition, nor did it possess actual or constructive notice of the condition with sufficient time to remedy it.
The Supreme Court granted the motion. We reverse.
